newsitem.title: FRANCE: French left has tough task keeping poll pledges.
newsitem.headline: French left has tough task keeping poll pledges.

text.p: For the French left, swept to power on Sunday in an upset election win, the hard part is yet to come.

Facing a public that analysts said voted more against the centre-right than for the left, the Socialists must act fast on a number of economic policy pledges if they are to win the confidence of France's disgruntled electorate.

Their room to manoeuvre will be limited, however, by a stated commitment to European economic and monetary union (EMU) and the need to meet tough economic criteria for a European single currency, planned to start on January 1, 1999.
Financial markets have served notice since the left pulled off a surprise first-round win a week ago that they are watching the election closely.
The French stock market lost 6.48 percent in the past week and bond and interest rate futures have been volatile, buffeted by worries about a left win.
The franc has weakened to about 3.38 per mark from about 3.36 before President Jacques Chirac announced the election.

Among the Socialists' biggest promise, and the one likely to be most dear to the French, was a pledge to create 700,000 jobs for the young, split evenly between the public and the private sector, paid for by scrapping existing jobs subsidies and without increasing overall public spending.

This pledge, combined with a vow not to subject the country to another round of austerity to qualify for EMU, seemed to be key vote-getters. A Socialist-led government may well feel under pressure to deliver.

After lambasting the government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe for raising the tax burden in France by about 120 billion francs ($20.7 billion), party leaders have vowed not to raise taxes or overall public spending.
"On the one hand, there is no question of raising total public spending. Secondly, there is no question of raising taxes," former prime minister Laurent Fabius said on Friday.
"There is some reorienting to do, but taxes need to be lowered, not raised. I am being completely clear," he added.
Another key Socialist promise was to cut the working week from 39 hours to 35 over the next two or three years without loss of salary.

As party leader Lionel Jospin has begun to scent victory over the past week, he has emphasised that most of the Socialists' promises will take time and that his government should be judged over the long haul.

"On the 35-hour week, it's not 35 hours right away," he told the daily Le Monde on May 29. "We have a three-year schedule, starting with a framework law, and then the opening of negotiations between social partners."

The Socialists have said they will maintain France's public service model. Under this model security, education, transport, health, post and telecommunications are services which must be guaranteed equally to all French people.
Consistent with this, the party said it does not plan to privatise France Telecom but then nuanced its position by saying it would consult the company's staff.
Many analysts said they believe the government will be forced to go ahead with a first tranche of the France Telecom sale to help finance some of its other economic programmes.
The party has left open the possibility of selling minority stakes in state-owned companies.
The party has also promised to shift payroll charges on to other taxes. It pledged to cut value-added tax (sales tax), lower housing tax and raise wealth tax.
And it has pledged to reform France's generous welfare system by negotiating control of health spending while ensuring free care for low-income households.
Jospin has said he will defend France's universal pension system and repeal a law passed by Juppe's government installing private pension funds.

The party said it would help entrepreneurs by developing a tax system favourable to risk investment for young companies and simplifying administrative procedures. It has also promised to re-establish administrative checks on company layoffs.
